description: How Elizabeth I ruled through her court, Privy Council, JPs and a Parliament she rarely called.
content_html:
Elizabeth I: Coronation and Early Reign

On 17 November 1558, Elizabeth I became Queen of England at the age of twenty-five. She was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 15 January 1559. Her accession was welcomed by many English people who had grown weary of the religious upheavals and foreign entanglements of her half-sister Mary I’s reign. Elizabeth was seen as a Protestant hope, young and English-born. Her early popularity was genuine — crowds lined the streets for her coronation procession, and she responded warmly, reportedly saying that the love of her subjects was more precious than any treasure.

Key Fact

Elizabeth was crowned on 15 January 1559. Within months she passed the Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity, establishing her control over the Church of England and setting the style of worship. This swift action showed her ability to govern decisively from the start of her reign.

The Royal Court

The Royal Court was the heart of Elizabethan government. It was wherever Elizabeth happened to be — at Whitehall Palace, Hampton Court, Greenwich or on one of her summer ‘progresses’ through the country. The court served two purposes: it was both a centre of pageantry designed to project royal power, and a practical arena where political decisions were made and favour was dispensed.

Nobles competed intensely to attend the Queen because proximity to Elizabeth meant access to patronage — the granting of offices, grants of land, or licences to trade. Those who lost favour could lose everything. This system gave Elizabeth enormous political leverage: she could reward loyalty and punish disloyalty simply by controlling access to her presence. Favourites such as Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, and later Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, gained influence through personal closeness to the Queen rather than formal office alone.

The Privy Council

The Privy Council was Elizabeth’s main governing body. It typically comprised around nineteen members — senior nobles, lawyers and churchmen — who met several times a week to advise the Queen, administer royal policy and handle correspondence. The Council had real power: it could issue proclamations, summon individuals for questioning and direct local officials.

The most influential councillor throughout much of Elizabeth’s reign was William Cecil, who served first as Secretary of State (1558–1572) and then as Lord Treasurer until his death in 1598. Cecil was cautious, Protestant and deeply loyal. He gathered intelligence through an extensive network of spies and helped Elizabeth navigate plots and crises. Elizabeth trusted him above all others, though she did not always follow his advice — particularly on the question of marriage and succession.

Sir Francis Walsingham served as Principal Secretary from 1573 until his death in 1590. A committed Puritan, he ran the government’s intelligence service and was responsible for uncovering the Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots against the Queen. Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, was Elizabeth’s favourite courtier and sat on the Council for many years; he commanded the English forces sent to the Netherlands in 1585. After Cecil’s death, his son Robert Cecil effectively took over the management of government, serving as Secretary of State from 1596 and eventually smoothing the succession of James VI of Scotland in 1603.

Local Government: Justices of the Peace

Beyond the court and Council, Elizabeth governed England through a network of Justices of the Peace. These were unpaid local gentlemen appointed by the Crown to serve in each county. By the end of the reign there were approximately 50–60 JPs in each county, and their responsibilities were vast: they enforced the law at quarter sessions, collected taxes, regulated wages, oversaw the poor relief system and ensured that royal proclamations were carried out.

The JP system was both the strength and the weakness of Elizabethan local government. It was cheap, and it bound the local gentry into the royal system — serving as a JP was a mark of social status that gentlemen competed for. However, the Crown depended on men it could not directly control. A JP who was sympathetic to Catholicism or reluctant to enforce unpopular policies could simply drag his feet. Elizabeth had no standing army or professional police force to enforce her will; she relied on willing cooperation.

Key Fact

Justices of the Peace were the backbone of Elizabethan local government — unpaid gentry who carried out royal orders in each county. Because they were unpaid and locally rooted, the Crown could not guarantee their full compliance, making local enforcement uneven.

Parliament: Role and Limitations

Parliament in Elizabethan England was very different from Parliament today. It had two chambers — the Lords (nobles and bishops) and the Commons (elected burgesses and knights of the shire) — but it was not a permanent institution. Elizabeth summoned Parliament only when she needed it, typically to grant taxation or to pass laws on matters that required its authority. During her forty-five-year reign she called Parliament only thirteen times, and for a total of fewer than four years in session.

Elizabeth was acutely aware of Parliament’s potential to challenge her authority. She refused to allow MPs to debate matters she considered her personal prerogative: religion, her marriage, and the succession. When Peter Wentworth raised the issue of free speech in Parliament in 1576, Elizabeth had him imprisoned in the Tower. She insisted that freedom of speech in Parliament meant freedom to discuss matters she had already introduced, not freedom to raise whatever MPs wished.

Parliament’s most important constitutional function was granting taxation. The Crown’s ordinary revenues — from royal estates, customs duties and feudal dues — were rarely sufficient to fund war or extraordinary expenditure. Elizabeth therefore called Parliament when she needed ‘subsidies’ voted by the Commons. Parliament used this power carefully; it could, in theory, refuse a subsidy or attach conditions. In practice, Elizabeth managed Parliament skillfully, using a network of ‘privy councillors’ who sat as MPs and managed debates. She also relied on the Speaker of the House of Commons (effectively a Crown appointee in this period) to steer business.
exam_tip_html: Questions about Elizabethan government often ask you to ‘describe two features’ of the Privy Council, Parliament or local government. For each feature, give a specific detail — not just “the Privy Council advised the Queen” but “the Privy Council met several times a week and could issue proclamations.” For 8-mark ‘Explain the significance’ questions, make sure you address both significance at the time AND significance over a longer period. William Cecil is a strong example for significance questions — his work shaped Elizabethan government for almost forty years. Avoid referring to boards or paper codes in your answers; just write ‘examiners’ or ‘the mark scheme.’
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Elizabeth governed through the Royal Court (patronage and favour), the Privy Council (policy and security, led by William Cecil) and a network of local Justices of the Peace who enforced royal orders in each county.
  • Parliament was summoned rarely — only thirteen times in forty-five years — mainly to grant taxation. Elizabeth strictly limited what MPs could debate, excluding her marriage, the succession and religion from parliamentary discussion.
  • The system depended heavily on the cooperation of the gentry (as JPs) and on Elizabeth’s personal skill in managing the court and council. The absence of a standing army or professional bureaucracy made willing compliance essential.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Privy Council in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Candidates may describe: the Privy Council comprised around nineteen members including nobles, lawyers and churchmen; it met several times a week; it could issue proclamations and direct local officials; William Cecil was its most influential figure. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature without specific detail (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of Justices of the Peace in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: a precise feature with accurate supporting detail (2 marks). Emerging: a simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: JPs were unpaid local gentry appointed by the Crown; they enforced the law at quarter sessions; they collected taxes; they oversaw poor relief; they enforced royal proclamations in the counties; approximately 50–60 JPs served in each county by the end of the reign. Maximum 4 marks (2 marks per feature).

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of tensions between Elizabeth I and Parliament.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed causal chain linking evidence to outcome, e.g. Elizabeth restricted parliamentary free speech because she considered her marriage, succession and religion to be royal prerogatives — this led to confrontations such as Peter Wentworth's imprisonment in 1576 when he pressed for unrestricted debate. Secure: a clear cause with some supporting evidence. Developing: a relevant cause with limited development. Emerging: a simple statement with minimal support. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of William Cecil to the government of Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (almost forty years of loyal service, managing foreign policy, intelligence networks, and the succession question) AND over time (securing Protestant England's survival as a stable state). Secure: clear explanation of significance with specific examples. Developing: some explanation with limited range of evidence. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a portrait of Elizabeth I at her coronation in 1559 for understanding how she projected royal authority in the early years of her reign? Use the source and your own knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the source shows), provenance (a formal royal commission, designed to project power) and contextual knowledge (Elizabeth used imagery deliberately — crowns, orbs, ermine — to emphasise legitimacy) to make a substantiated judgement about utility and limitations. Secure: addresses two of the three elements. Developing: mainly describes source content. Emerging: simple comment on one element. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'Elizabeth I was successful in governing England in the years 1558–1603 because of the effectiveness of the Privy Council.' How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your own knowledge to evaluate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: agrees with evidence (Cecil's management of plots and foreign policy; the Council's role in proclamations and administration) AND disagrees with evidence (Elizabeth's personal skill in court management and patronage; the JP system; Parliament's role in taxation) before reaching a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides covered with some supporting detail; clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided or limited evidence. Emerging: simple agreement or disagreement. Maximum 12 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: Who was Elizabeth I's most trusted councillor for nearly forty years, serving as Secretary of State and later Lord Treasurer?
How many times did Elizabeth I call Parliament during her forty-five-year reign?
Justices of the Peace were unpaid local _____ appointed by the Crown to enforce law and royal orders in each county.
The Royal Court was wherever Elizabeth happened to be, and courtiers competed for her _____, which gave access to offices and grants of land.
Match each Elizabethan institution to its key function:
right: Met several times a week to advise the Queen and issue proclamations
Enforced royal orders and maintained law in the counties
Granted taxation and passed laws when summoned by the Crown

flashcard_questions.q: When was Elizabeth I crowned Queen of England?
What was the main purpose of the Royal Court in Elizabethan government?
flashcard_questions.a: To project royal power and dispense patronage to loyal nobles and courtiers.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was William Cecil and why was he significant?
flashcard_questions.a: Elizabeth's principal adviser; served as Secretary of State then Lord Treasurer for nearly forty years.

flashcard_questions.q: What role did Francis Walsingham play in Elizabeth's government?
flashcard_questions.a: He ran the government's intelligence service and uncovered several Catholic plots against Elizabeth.

flashcard_questions.q: How many members typically sat on Elizabeth's Privy Council?
What were Justices of the Peace and who were they?
flashcard_questions.a: Unpaid local gentry appointed by the Crown to enforce law and royal orders in each county.

flashcard_questions.q: The Elizabethan system relied on JPs, yet they could be unreliable. Why?
flashcard_questions.a: They were unpaid and locally rooted, so the Crown could not guarantee their full compliance.

flashcard_questions.q: How often did Elizabeth I summon Parliament during her reign?
flashcard_questions.a: Only thirteen times in forty-five years, totalling fewer than four years in session.

flashcard_questions.q: What matters did Elizabeth refuse to allow Parliament to debate?
flashcard_questions.a: Her marriage, the succession, and religion — all considered royal prerogatives.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was imprisoned in the Tower in 1576 for pressing Parliament's right to free speech?
What was Parliament's most important constitutional function?
flashcard_questions.a: Granting taxation (subsidies) to fund royal expenditure, especially for war.

flashcard_questions.q: The ____ of ____ was Elizabeth's most trusted councillor, serving from 1558 until his death in 1598.

glossary_terms.definition: Queen of England from 1558 to 1603, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, the last Tudor monarch.
The household of the monarch, comprising nobles, courtiers and officials who competed for royal favour and patronage.
A group of the monarch's most trusted advisers who met regularly to discuss policy, administer royal decisions and handle security matters.
Elizabeth's principal Secretary of State and later Lord Treasurer, her most trusted adviser for nearly forty years.
Unpaid local gentry appointed by the Crown to maintain law and order, collect taxes and enforce royal proclamations in their counties.
